articles.title: Discord might use AI to help you catch up on conversations
articles.summary: Discord has become the place for gaming communities on the internet. It just celebrated its 10th anniversary. But as it tries to grow, one of the big challenges it faces is that it isn’t a good replacement for forums.
articles.body: Discord has become the place for gaming communities on the internet. The company just celebrated its 10th anniversary, and its impact is now big enough that it’s available directly on PlayStation and Xbox and was ripped off by Nintendo for the Switch 2’s GameChat. But as it tries to grow, one of the big challenges Discord faces is that, for big or longer-running communities, it can be hard to know where to start, hard to catch up to the speed of real-time conversations, and hard to sift through the potentially huge amounts of conversations and channels. A lot of communities used to form around forums, but Discord just isn’t a good replacement for that kind of structured messaging, as covered by Aftermath’s Luke Plunkett. “This is something we want to solve,” Peter Sellis, Discord’s SVP of product, tells The Verge. “It is not our intention to lock a bunch of this knowledge into Discord.” One way Discord wants to tackle the problem is add features that are “more amicable to structured knowledge sharing, like forums, that we could probably do a better job of investing in and is something we want to do for game developers,” Sellis says. Another involves LLMs. “There’s an incredible opportunity now with large language models and their ability to summarize conversations,” he says. That could help Discord take a long conversation between multiple people — “what is essentially a really poorly structured shareable object,” he says — and boil it down to “something that could be more shareable and then potentially syndicated to the web.” Sellis couldn’t share many other details, and couldn’t give a timeline for when any of this might be ready: “I haven’t seen a solution that we feel great about yet.” Discord wants to do it right, he says — especially because a solution that makes information more easily accessible outside of Discord could involve a lot of work for server moderators and admins. “We have a very sensitive radar for stuff that causes them a bunch of work that doesn’t give them the return they need,” he says. (It’s wise not to piss off your moderators.) None of this was imminent, if it even happens at all. That said, “I assure you that this is something that people within Discord feel the pain of themselves,” Sellis says. “And when our engineers and product designers and product managers feel it personally, they generally want to solve it.” Another big challenge Discord faces is how to build the product to serve both the needs of giant community servers and the tiny servers where groups hang out — especially when, according to Discord, 90 percent of “all activity on Discord” happens in “small, intimate servers.” Sellis calls it “one of the biggest challenges for the team” — but also says that it’s “honestly the biggest opportunity.” He says that Discord thinks about how it can make people “feel comfortable in both these spaces, understand that there are different types of spaces, and the technology is familiar, but still different in both of these places.” Sellis says that the biggest Discord server is Midjourney, a key company in text-to-AI image generation that lets you generate visuals right inside Discord. Midjourney became popular because it turned the “single-player game” of generating AI images into a multiplayer community. “You can just watch people try things, experiment, fail, succeed, embarrass themselves, etc. And that made it kind of like a collective action.” He says Discord is seeing something similar with the recently launched Wordle app on the platform, too, which lets you compete with your friends. That all speaks to some of Discord’s larger vision. Sellis is seeing a trend that “everything is starting to kind of look like a game” and “Discord can be used as a social layer on any game to essentially improve its engagement, its socialness, and its multiplayer capacity. That’s something we like and are going to lean into.” And as for Nintendo’s GameChat? “I would say imitation is a very sincere form of flattery,” Sellis says. “Hard to imagine being more flattered than being copied by Nintendo.”

articles.title: Cosméticos com frutos da Amazônia: jovens do AP inovam no skincare | G1
articles.standfirst: Startup nascida na Unifap usa copaíba, murumuru e açaí para desenvolver produtos de skincare. Grupo já vende para todo o país.
articles.summary: Startup da Unifap cria cosméticos com frutos da Amazônia e tecnologia coreana, desenvolvendo produtos de skincare que já são vendidos para todo o país.
articles.body:
Com tecnologia inspirada na Coreia, jovens do AP criam linha de cosméticos com frutos da Amazônia — Foto: Lenan Santos/Rede Amazônica

A rotina de cuidados com a pele (skincare) inspirada na indústria da Coreia do Sul virou tendência mundial. No Amapá , um grupo de estudantes e recém-formados no curso de Farmácia da Universidade Federal do Amapá (Unifap) resolveu utilizar a mesma tecnologia oriental, mas com um diferencial regional: ativos extraídos de plantas e frutos da floresta amazônica.

A ideia da startup Tropicácia nasceu durante uma maratona de inovação universitária, o Amapá Startup, e ganhou força nos laboratórios da instituição.

O grupo, que começou a trajetória na empresa júnior do curso, decidiu transformar o conhecimento acadêmico em um negócio independente.

"As indústrias coreanas usam os nossos ativos para desenvolver os cosméticos delas. Então nada nos impede de utilizar a tecnologia de ponta para desenvolvermos os produtos aqui mesmo", afirmou a farmacêutica e CEO da marca, Saile Lacerda.

Farmacêutica e CEO da marca, Saile Lacerda — Foto: Lenan Santos/Rede Amazônica

A linha de produtos inclui itens como gloss labial, velas de massagem, blends de argila e a espuma de limpeza facial, carro-chefe da marca, desenvolvida com essência de açaí e propriedades calmantes para a pele.

Para garantir o fornecimento das matérias-primas, os estudantes compram óleos e manteigas vegetais diretamente de produtores e comunidades extrativistas do estado, como no arquipélago do Bailique e no município de Mazagão.

Entenda os ativos amazônicos usados nos produtos:

🌿 Copaíba : óleo extraído do tronco da árvore, conhecido pela ação anti-inflamatória e cicatrizante.

🌴 Murumuru : manteiga tirada da semente da palmeira, com alto poder de hidratação.

💧 Pracaxi : óleo típico de áreas de várzea, indicado para regeneração e proteção da pele.

🌳 Açaí e Cupuaçu : frutos regionais ricos em antioxidantes, usados para nutrição e aroma.

"É uma forma de devolver para a sociedade o que aprendemos na universidade. Priorizamos os fornecedores locais para movimentar a economia circular e valorizar a riqueza do Amapá ", ressaltou Saile.

Antes de chegar ao consumidor, cada formulação passa por testes de estabilidade, avaliação sensorial (textura e aroma) e verificação de segurança em relação às normas da Agência Nacional de Vigilância Sanitária (Anvisa).

Apesar do crescimento e de premiações em editais de inovação, o grupo enfrenta gargalos comuns às pequenas empresas da região: a falta de infraestrutura industrial local para produção em larga escala. Por isso, os lotes ainda são manipulados de forma artesanal e manual.

Gloss labial da marca. — Foto: Lenan Santos/Rede Amazônica

Mesmo com os desafios de mercado, as vendas já ultrapassaram as fronteiras do estado por meio de plataformas digitais e do comércio eletrônico.

"Criamos a startup recentemente e ver que já estamos construindo um caminho tão sólido é emocionante. Saber que pessoas de fora valorizam um produto feito aqui com a nossa biodiversidade traz muito orgulho", comemorou a estudante de Farmácia Yasmin Santos.

Grupo começou a trajetória na empresa júnior do curso — Foto: Lenan Santos/Rede Amazônica

articles.title: Former OpenAI science lead launches Warp Science to automate wet labs with robots | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Wearing cameras and sensor gloves, the startup’s human chemists will train robots to perform various lab tasks.
articles.body:
Former OpenAI science lead Kevin Weil has launched Warp Sciences, a new AI startup focused on automating lab work for drug discovery. The company, which trains robots to make and test promising compounds identified by researchers, has raised $215 million at an $865 million valuation, according to Weil, who announced the startup and funding on X.

The round was led by Lightspeed, with participation from IVP, Premji Invest, and Lux Capital.

For years, biotech companies have outsourced the most labor-intensive work of synthesizing thousands of variations of molecules to contractors in China, such as WuXi AppTec. With Warp Sciences, Weil hopes to reshore that work and insulate the entire drug development process from geopolitical supply-chain risks.

Wearing cameras and sensor gloves, the startup’s human chemists will train robots to perform various lab tasks. By automating wet-lab work, Warp Sciences aims to accelerate drug discovery using robots that can operate around the clock.

articles.title: Discord now formats Markdown previews right
articles.summary: Discord’s latest update released today has a big improvement for Markdown previews: they should now render correctly instead of with “a bunch of symbols,” according to the company.
articles.body: Discord’s latest update released today has a big improvement for Markdown previews: they should now render correctly instead of with “a bunch of symbols,” according to the company. LLMs and AI agents often rely on Markdown files for instructions and context, so these improved previews could be helpful for people sharing information about AI projects on the platform. “When you upload a Markdown (.md) file, you’ll now see the file rendered all nice and neat and pretty instead of with a bunch of symbols,” Discord says. “This includes tables, formatting, all that good stuff. Totally great for when you’re doing a casual Sunday-night sharing READMEs with your friends.” Google has also improved its Markdown support, as it recently started letting users edit Markdown files directly in Docs without having to convert the files to the Docs format. Discord says its new update also lets you organize servers and channels by right-clicking the icon on the sidebar and using a new “Move to…” feature. Discord Nitro members are also now able to upload files as large as 1GB.

articles.title: The secret to fast startup growth isn't early sales, top names in tech say | TechCrunch
articles.summary: At this year’s Disrupt, Lovable GTM lead Luke Arno, Polsia's Ben Broca, and Theory Ventures’ Tomasz Tunguz gave founders some tips on how to achieve true sales success in the first 90 days.
articles.body:
The AI era has changed how fast startups can grow. Startups can grow so fast that they hit high annual recurring revenue (ARR) numbers, only to crash and burn a few months later. At this year’s TechCrunch Disrupt , Lovable go-to-market lead Luke Arno, Ben Broca of the AI platform Polsia, and Theory Ventures’ Tomasz Tunguz gave founders some tips on how to set their companies up for success in those first 90 days.

Broca, whose company Polsia uses AI agents to build and run businesses with almost no human staff (Broca says he is its only employee), said that product-market fit is one of the hardest things to find right now, especially in an era when so many products can easily be copied by competitors. In response, Arno said that durable go-to-market strategies are those that can be reliably repeated.

“The most critical thing for founders or earlier-stage companies to do is develop learning density or pattern recognition for where your customers are,” Arno said. “Don’t rush to build out a top-down go-to-market motion if you’re not there yet.”

That’s why, in those first 90 days after launching a commercial product that’s ready to sell, founders should not mistake early, fast revenue for a sign that the startup is ready to scale, Arno said.

Once a startup finds use cases that work, it will only be ready to build out a sales team and go for growth after it can attract new customers by repeating what has worked. If every sale requires new tactics, the startup hasn’t truly hit product-market fit.

“If I bring on 10 new customers in 10 different ways to solve 10 different problems, sure, I brought revenue in, but I don’t have a way to go scale a go-to-market,” Arno said. “If I bring three customers in with a similar motion to solve a similar problem, now I have high confidence that I can go scale.”

Lovable, the AI app-building startup, set a lot of those early benchmarks with how fast it grew, and now founders everywhere are feeling the pressure to do the same. Lovable is valued at more than $13 billion by its investors, says its ARR has passed $600 million, and has raised more than $700 million in funding to date.

“The expectations for overall execution speed are absolutely tremendous,” Tunguz said.

But Tunguz said growth like Lovable’s is still the exception, though founders should still move fast. The pressure they feel is real, he said, because far more money flows through the startup ecosystem at every stage than when he began investing in 2008. Today, a seed deal brought in by one of his partners could just as easily be a $5 million raise, a $50 million raise, or a $500 million raise.

The winners all focus on one thing: understanding their customers well enough to know what will keep them around even after any hype subsides.

“Community building is very important and being close to customers is very important,” Broca said. He said founders can send emails and throw events, and he personally likes to talk to a lot of his customers: “The general rule is always to be talking to customers.”

articles.title: Arc browser sunsets December 22 as The Browser Company doubles down on Dia | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Arc was fiercely beloved by a dedicated group of enthusiasts, but it never quite became the mass-market Chrome alternative its makers once envisioned.
articles.body:
The Browser Company is sunsetting its design-forward Arc browser on December 22, 2026, and directing users to Dia, its AI-first browser. The company announced the decision on Thursday, citing the rising cost of keeping a browser secure in the age of AI.

“Keeping a browser secure takes constant, dedicated work that is only increasing in the age of AI,” the company wrote.

“Dia was built from the ground up to meet today’s security standards, so that’s where our engineering and security teams will focus moving forward.”

The wind-down is staged into three parts. As of Thursday, new Arc accounts can no longer be created. On November 23, Arc Search on iOS and Android will lose its AI features, including “Browse for Me.” Users will no longer be able to sign in or sync tabs, though the app will continue functioning as a basic local browser.

On December 22, Arc will stop working entirely on Mac and Windows. Accounts will be deactivated, and personal data will be deleted within 30 days. Arc Search will also be removed from the Google Play Store.

While The Browser Company claims Dia now surpasses Arc in speed, stability, and security benchmarks, user reactions on social media were largely disappointed , with many reviving requests for the company to make Arc open source.

But CEO Josh Miller previously pointed out that Arc is built on the Arc Development Kit (ADK) — a proprietary internal SDK that is also the core engine powering Dia. Open-sourcing Arc would mean giving away Dia’s intellectual property.

“While we’d love to open-source Arc someday, we can’t do that meaningfully without also open-sourcing ADK,” Miller previously noted. “And ADK is still core to our company’s value.”

For users making the switch, Dia will carry over equivalents of several core Arc features. Users can still swipe between different work and personal environments using Dia’s “Profiles” (formerly Arc’s Spaces). Arc’s signature vertical tabs will remain as an optional sidebar layout, while Folders have been rebranded as “Pinned Tab Groups.”

Passwords, bookmarks, extensions, and history will seamlessly transfer to Dia. Arc features will remain free in Dia, with AI optional.

The shutdown officially closes a chapter that began in 2025, when the startup stopped active feature development on Arc. The Browser Company — which was acquired by Atlassian for $610 million in 2025 — conceded at the time that while early adopters loved the browser’s novel interface, the “ novelty tax ” and complexity limited mainstream adoption. Arc was fiercely beloved by a dedicated group of enthusiasts, but it never quite became the mass-market Chrome alternative its makers once envisioned.

articles.title: Rivian buys world model startup to accelerate self-driving ambitions | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Third Dimension's technology uses AI to match the physical world, which when combined with Rivian's reams of data could turn into a valuable simulator.
articles.body:
EV maker Rivian has acquired Third Dimension, a U.K. startup founded by veterans of the gaming and autonomous vehicle industries that uses AI to turn images and videos into lifelike 3D worlds.

Rivian isn’t getting into gaming, but it does want to leverage Third Dimension’s technology to turn real-world data into 3D worlds that can accelerate the development of its advanced driver-assistance features and the self-driving system for the robotaxis it plans to supply to Uber.

Terms of the deal were not disclosed. The 15-person team at Third Dimension, most of whom are based in the U.K., will be absorbed into Rivian’s autonomy and AI team led by James Philbin. The acquisition also gives Rivian an opportunity to expand its AI hub in London, Philbin said in an exclusive interview.

Third Dimension, which was founded by CEO Tolga Kart and Piotr Sokólski in 2024, raised $7 million in seed funding from venture capital firms, including Abstract Ventures, MVP, Soma Capital, and Solari Capital. While the company’s technology was built to speed up video game development, the founders saw other potential applications, including defense and autonomous vehicles.

Now, under Rivian, they’ll be focused on automated driving.

“The team is excited to be able to focus on one problem,” Kart told TechCrunch in the interview. “I think as a small company, having to serve many, many different masters is very hard, and so we’re very excited to come work on a problem that has such an amount of scale, where our technology makes a true difference.”

Simulation is a critical tool for autonomous vehicle developers, who use it to train and validate self-driving systems. Historically, these simulators were built on rendering or video game engines and often relied on synthetic data. These virtual environments might look like the real world, but a gap between the two remains, Kart said. The workaround typically requires feeding the simulators ever-larger amounts of data in hopes of closing that quality gap.

Third Dimension’s technology uses AI to match the physical world, which when combined with Rivian’s reams of data could turn into a valuable simulator.

Rivian collects driving data from tens of thousands of R1S pickup trucks, R1S SUVs, delivery vans, and R2 SUVs on the road today — essentially any vehicle whose owner has enabled external camera sharing. Rivian uses that data, which is aggregated and anonymized, to build training models for driving. According to Philbin, Rivian gets more than 400,000 sequences uploaded from its customer fleets per day.

Third Dimension’s tech will allow Rivian to simulate complex driving conditions without having to wait for rare real-world edge cases to occur, Philbin said.

This story is developing and will be updated.

articles.title: OpenAI working on new $30B raise at $1.25T valuation ahead of IPO | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Should OpenAI command an over $1 trillion valuation with this round, it would break records as the most highly valued private company ever.
articles.body:
OpenAI is reportedly close to securing another mega round of private funding, rather than plowing ahead with an IPO. The AI lab is working on raising up to $30 billion at a $1.25 trillion pre-money valuation in a round led by Coatue and investors in UAE, sources told CNBC .

This follows a similar report by Bloomberg a month ago which said the AI lab was working on raising $30 billion at a $1.4 trillion valuation. Terms are still being negotiated, both outlets report, so they could ultimately change. CNBC reports that the UAE funding could also be coupled with a deal to secure more computing capacity for OpenAI from the UAE, too. OpenAI declined comment.

Should OpenAI command a valuation of more than $1 trillion with this round, it would break records as the most valued private company ever. That valuation would also raise the bar even higher for OpenAI’s forthcoming IPO. OpenAI filed confidential paperwork for an IPO in June, after its last raise in March valued the ChatGPT maker at $852 billion post-money .

That high valuation could also have ramifications for Anthropic’s IPO, which many believe is closer to materializing. (Rumors suggest we could see Anthropic’s public S-1 filing any day now.) The latest reports have Anthropic seeking a $1.5 to $2 trillion valuation for its public debut, CNBC reports. Anthropic raised $65 billion at a $965 billion valuation in May in what many believed at the time would be its last big round before an IPO. It also filed confidential paperwork in June.

articles.title: As blockchain investing falls out of vogue, a16z Crypto rebrands as a16z Frontier | TechCrunch
articles.summary: The digital asset unit, helmed by Chris Dixon, broadens its scope.
articles.body:
In a sign that crypto and blockchain-focused investing has receded in importance, Andreessen Horowitz announced Thursday that it is renaming its digital asset unit from a16z Crypto to a16z Frontier.

The practice, helmed by Chris Dixon, has raised nearly $10 billion across five funds since launching in 2018, backing some of the sector’s biggest wins, including Coinbase. Yet for years, a16z and rival venture firms struggled to push crypto’s utility beyond financial rails, trading applications, and speculative assets.

Under the new name, the team is broadening its mandate to focus on emerging technologies, be it AI, robotics, or “new kinds of networks” connecting humans and machines. Yet, the group isn’t abandoning crypto. Dixon wrote in a blog post that blockchain technology could “give new networks native economic capabilities.”

Alongside Dixon, a16z Frontier’s general partners include Eddy Lazzarin and Guy Wuollet. Meanwhile, Ali Yahya, who joined the crypto strategy as its first investor in 2017, has left the firm, according to The Information .

articles.title: Warhound raises $200M to engineer war dogs and arm them with Anduril gear | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Warhound, the brainchild of Ben Lamm and Palmer Luckey, emerges from stealth to genetically engineer dogs for military and law enforcement.
articles.body:
Colossal Biosciences’ Ben Lamm and Andruil’s Palmer Luckey had an idea to genetically engineer war dogs for the U.S. military, law enforcement, and other emergency response teams. That idea, on Thursday, announced its emergence from stealth as Warhound , armed with $200 million in funding from investors including In-Q-Tel, Sequoia, and 8VC. The round values the company at $1.2 billion.

These are dogs that perform tasks that are dangerous for humans or difficult for machines, like bomb detection, searches, and other specialized operations. In its launch announcement, the company said that more than 80% of the working dogs used by the U.S. military come from Europe and less than half of them are fit for service.

So not only is there a dwindling supply of working dogs for these tasks, but the U.S. has also become increasingly reliant on foreign nations for dogs that play an important role in the U.S. military and in law enforcement. That is key for what Warhound is trying to do. The hope is that Colossal can use its technology to engineer dogs with “characteristics suited to demanding missions,” the company said in a press release.

Lamm told TechCrunch he met Luckey about a year ago at a conference, where the Anduril co-founder brought up doing more for working dogs in the U.S. military. The two kept in touch, and Lamm did more research, learning about the breeding issues. Many dogs do not make it through training because of genetic dispositions for issues like poor eyesight or the high possibilities of cancer, hip dysplasia, or muscle atrophy.

Lamm believed dogs could be enhanced for health, longevity, and “for things like speed and agility or enhance olfactory sensors for bomb sniffing and whatnot,” he said. His team looked at the top-performing working dog breeds — the Belgian Malinois and German Shepherd — taking the cell lines from them and putting them in a biobank. From there, they will edit the genes, adding the ones that will make the dogs perform better while taking out the ones that won’t, to create “a new type of dog.”

Andruil, meanwhile, will provide software and hardware enhancement for items such as dog protection vests and eye goggles to assist the dogs and their handlers with matters like situational awareness and coordination.

He said to imagine, for example, bulletproof vests that have data sensors that give information back to the handlers so they can better understand what is happening.

“The idea is, if we make the dog safer, make it healthier, make it perform better, it’s going to perform better in the line of duty,” Lamm said. He added that Anduril’s additions aim to make the dogs safer and healthier outside of their genetic components, “on top of the dog, not in the dog.” He believes such enhancements will also protect the dogs’ human handlers better.

Luckey doesn’t own equity in the company and is only a partner, Lamm told TechCrunch, clarifying that Colossal owns equity in the business, which it supports with licensing its technology.

Colossal is currently known for its de-extinction efforts of animals like the dodo and the mammoth . As Lamm previously told TechCrunch, the company has been using AI, buying and building technology to help with gene cloning and the identification and reproduction of animal genes.

The first batch of dogs is about to be cloned and incubated and is expected to be born early next year, ideally entering service within the next two years, Lamm said. Another company owned by Colossal, Viagen, is partnering with Warhound to help clone the dogs. Lamm said Viagen’s tech has a high success rate with cloning, and Colossal currently uses it for its program to help protect endangered species.

The startup doesn’t know yet how much it will charge for the dogs but expects to sell to parties like first responders, the Department of Defense, military service groups, and police forces. When asked about government approval, Lamm said the company has briefed many government groups about the business.

In terms of the responsibility and safety of civilians when it comes to releasing genetically enhanced dogs, Lamm said the dog will be trained like any military working dog and will be managed by whoever buys it.

The company said it is working under the guidance of the American Humane Society to help certify Warhound’s training program for the newly created dogs that will enter service. The hope is also that when these new military dogs retire, they will enter the Society’s Military Working Dog Reunification Program, which provides a home for retired military dogs — or another program the society offers to help dogs.

articles.title: What some of Anthropic’s backers are reportedly worth before its IPO
articles.summary: Early-stage and follow-on investors in the AI lab are already sitting on major paper returns.
articles.body:
Anthropic’s public listing, which is expected this year at a valuation of as much as $2 trillion, is bound to be a windfall for both early-stage and later-stage investors. But even at the company’s latest private market valuation of $965 billion, the stakes held by many of those VCs and early backers already total billions. Here is what some backers in the leading AI lab are worth at that last round’s price, according to Bloomberg :

Eric Schmidt: The former Google CEO invested in Anthropic’s Series A in 2021, when the startup was valued at $461 million, according to PitchBook data. Today, Schmidt owns about 1% of the company, and even at its current private valuation, his stake is worth nearly $10 billion.

Iconiq: The investment outfit wrote a $6 billion check to Anthropic last year when the company was already valued at $183 billion. That massive late-stage bet is now worth $17 billion and has the potential to double at the IPO.

Menlo Ventures: The VC firm led Anthropic’s Series D and has invested more than $1 billion in the company over time, a stake now worth $14 billion.

Sequoia: The famed VC firm backed the AI lab for the first time only earlier this year, when the company was already valued at $380 billion. The $3 billion investment gave it about 1% ownership, which means it has already more than doubled its investment.

Sound Ventures: The firm, launched by Guy Oseary and actor Ashton Kutcher, invested $35 million in Anthropic’s 2023 Series C round and has since funneled an additional $400 million into the company, resulting in a stake that’s worth billions now. (Kutcher left Sound Ventures this year to launch a new VC firm .)

Spark Capital: The only VC firm known to hold a board seat at Anthropic invested $75 million in that same 2023 Series C round, when it was valued at $5 billion. That position has ballooned more than ninetyfold to $7 billion.

articles.title: Agent cloud startup Daytona hits $1B valuation backed by FirstMark and a who’s who of angels | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Daytona is building a cloud for agents that's like giving every agent its own computer. It has attracted founders of Stripe, Perplextity, Datadog, Mercor, and others as angels, it says.
articles.body:
Daytona Platforms announced on Friday that it had raised a $60 million Series B round at a $1 billion valuation led by FirstMark Growth. The company says it has now raised a total of $91 million.

The New York-based startup has attracted not just FirstMark (which also led its $24 million Series A in February), but also a host of well-known angels in this latest round. Daytona says they include Stripe’s Patrick Collison, Shopify’s Tobi Lütke, Perplexity’s Aravind Srinivas, Zoom’s Eric Yuan, Datadog’s Olivier Pomel, Quora’s Adam D’Angelo (who is also an OpenAI board member), and Mercor’s Brendan Foody. It also names Qualcomm Ventures, Samsung Next, and Okta Ventures as participants.

Three-year-old Daytona is building a cloud specifically for long-running agents, which have different infrastructure needs than yesteryear’s software, the startup contends. “Agents don’t work like the long-lived services today’s cloud was designed for. They spin up thousands of short, stateful jobs nobody planned in advance, and they need a cloud built for that,” founder Ivan Burazin wrote in a blog post announcing the new round . Daytona’s cloud, he said, is like giving every agent its own computer, where agents have access to sandboxed versions of Linux, Windows, macOS, and GPUs, among other services, on the one platform.

Building a startup means making decisions before you have all the answers.

When should you scale? How do you know you really have product-market fit? What does it take to land enterprise customers? How do you build the right team? And when you finally get in front of an investor, how do you make sure your pitch earns another conversation?

Some of the speakers founders will hear from in Boston

Steve Fredette on building a company that keeps reinventing itself

Boston founders do not have to look far for an example of what can happen when a startup finds its market and continues evolving with its customers.

Steve Fredette , president, co-founder, and director of Toast , takes the Impact Stage for “Building a Company That Keeps Reinventing Itself.”

Toast’s story offers founders a compelling case study in identifying a customer problem, finding product-market fit, winning customers, and ultimately scaling a Boston startup into a public company.

But reaching scale does not mean the work is finished. Fredette’s conversation will look at what it takes to continue evolving a company as customer expectations, technology, and the market change around it, while staying connected to the needs that helped create the business in the first place.

Kent Bennett on knowing when product-market fit is real

Growth can be exciting. Growing too early can be expensive.

Kent Bennett , partner at Bessemer Venture Partners , will lead “Finding Product Market Fit Before You Scale,” focusing on one of the most important questions an early-stage founder can answer: Are customers actually telling you that you are ready to grow?

The session will give founders a chance to think more critically about the signals that matter before adding headcount, increasing spend, or accelerating go-to-market efforts.

It is a useful counterpoint to startup culture’s constant pressure to move faster. Sometimes the smartest next move is making sure the foundation is actually there.

Rudina Seseri on when to scale and when to hit the brakes

That same tension takes center stage with Rudina Seseri , founder and managing partner of Glasswing Ventures .

In “When to Scale and When to Hit the Brakes,” Seseri will explore how founders can distinguish between the moments that call for acceleration and the moments when restraint may protect the business.

Founders are constantly making trade-offs between growth and discipline. Knowing when not to scale can be just as consequential as knowing when to go all in.

Lior Div on building for AI from day one

AI is reshaping how new companies think about products, operations, and teams, but adding AI to an existing process is different from building a company around it from the start.

Lior Div , CEO and co-founder of 7AI , will tackle that distinction in “Built for AI From Day One.”

For founders building in the current technology environment, the conversation provides an opportunity to think beyond AI as a feature and toward how it can influence the architecture and operating model of an entire company.

Chase Garbarino on the Boston founder playbook

The startup world does not begin and end in Silicon Valley.

Chase Garbarino , CEO and co-founder of HqO , will take the Impact Stage for “The Boston Founder Playbook,” examining what it means to build and scale a company from Boston.

For founders across New England and the broader East Coast ecosystem, the conversation offers a particularly relevant perspective on talent, customers, capital, and community outside the Bay Area.

Combined with Fredette’s Toast story, it also gives this year’s Summit a strong local through line: Ambitious companies can be built in Boston, and founders here do not need to copy Silicon Valley to do it.

Dave Balter on the pitch that gets you another meeting

A pitch does not have to close the deal. It has to make someone want the next conversation.

Dave Balter , venture partner at True Ventures and CEO of Edisyl , will explore that idea in “Your Pitch Has to Earn the Next Conversation.”

For founders accustomed to explaining their companies every day, the session is a reminder that knowing your business and communicating its story are two different skills.

Later in the afternoon, attendees will see that theory put into practice.

articles.title: Carta and NewView partner, hoping to entice more startups to let employees sell shares early | TechCrunch
articles.summary: A new program wants to encourage more startups to allow workers to cash out early by making it easier to transact tender offers.
articles.body:
Startups are staying private longer, leaving employees, who typically take a portion of their compensation as stock they can’t sell, with little hope of early liquidity.

An increasing number of late-stage startups are recognizing this and offering tender offers to employees. These are transactions that allow employees (and, often, early investors) to sell a portion of their shares for a predetermined price to an approved investor.

To simplify the tender process, NewView Capital recently partnered with Carta. The collaboration combines NewView’s secondary deal-structuring experience with Carta’s equity platform. Ravi Viswanathan, founder and managing partner of NewView, pitches this as a way to help startups launch and manage liquidity programs more seamlessly.

“The hope is that this partnership will make it easier for CEOs and companies to think about tenders,” he said. He wants founders to think about giving employees early liquidity as a “win-win-win” for workers, companies, and investors alike.

A growing number of startups seem to agree. Over the past three years, tender offers increased threefold for Series C and later-stage startups, according to a recent study from NewView and Carta. Plus, the startups that do choose tender offers are no longer just the most valuable private companies, like OpenAI, Databricks, or Anduril, according to Viswanathan.

For instance, last year, his firm, which specializes in secondary deals along with typical venture investments, helped facilitate a tender for Hightouch at a $1.3 billion valuation, when the marketing customization startup was seven years old.

However, Carta and NewView also found that the overall share of startups launching these offerings remains relatively small, with just 44 executed in the first half of 2026. So Viswanathan wants to encourage other startups to consider tender offers, calling them excellent retention tools and morale boosters.

A decade ago, being a unicorn was enough to attract talent, Viswanathan said, but with so many billion-dollar companies around today, that status may not be as much of a draw now. Offering a tender, he said, “is an opportunity to say you will also get liquidity in your journey with us.”

Some of the companies that recently held tender offers include AI customer support startup Decagon , self-driving tech developer Wayve , and AI voice generator ElevenLabs , which executed two such offerings in less than a year.

“The companies are staying private for 12 to 15 years. That’s not changing,” Viswanathan said. “In that interim, so that we don’t have this talent drain from high-quality venture-backed companies into their public counterparts, we need to make sure that there is liquidity for the employees.”

articles.title: VCs, Superhuman Mail founder share red flags about product-market fit | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Top investors from Iconiq and Sapphire Ventures, along with Rahul Vohra, the founder of Superhuman Mail, share the do's and don'ts for building hit products.
articles.body:
Product-market fit — when a startup’s product sells well — has become even harder to find in this AI era. Despite startups achieving record-fast growth, not all customers are sticky and products can be replicated more easily than ever.

Anu Bharadwaj, a partner at Iconiq; Rajeev Dham, a partner at Sapphire Ventures; and Rahul Vohra, the founder of Superhuman Mail, discussed the new rules for product-market fit last week at TechCrunch Disrupt .

“It’s never been easier to gain a bunch of pilots because lots of companies across the board are open to trying new things,” Bharadwaj said to the audience. “But going from pilot to production is really the hard thing.”

Right now, she said, a lot of founders pitch revenue metrics to investors without specifying which revenue they are talking about. “Is it true ARR or is it run rate?” she said. “There’s many ways to obfuscate the whole thing.”

Lately, much chatter on X has focused on AI founders inflating ARR numbers (which could mean “annualized run rate” or the more solid “annual recurring revenue”) to make it seem like their companies are doing better than they are. A common gimmick is counting pilot customers, who might only use the product for a couple of months, in the annualized run rate revenue number, implying that income is expected to continue for the entire year.

It should be obvious, but Bharadwaj pointed out, “It’s definitely in your long-term interest that you be very honest and upfront about what quality of revenue this is.”

She said companies need to separate hype from reality when looking at the quality of their revenue. It’s a red flag, for example, if only a few customers make up much of a company’s revenue or if the customers can easily go to another vendor for a better price. “Churn rate and retention [are] really dependent on that,” she continued.

That’s why Vohra advises startups to track customer engagement and dollar retention, especially for consumer products. “Figure out what benchmark [is] good, great, and excellent for your space,” he said.

For example, at Superhuman, he said that the company tracked ARR but also had their own internal metric called “delighted ARR,” which, he said, “was the ARR only from customers who are super engaged with the product.” He said that metric helped them see how sticky the customers were and how long they were likely to stay around.

“Those users are now still users, those companies are now still customers,” he continued. “We obsessed over serving that particular category of our user base and our customer base.”

The panelists also discussed green flags that indicate a startup has indeed found product-market fit. For Vohra, he said talk to customers to understand what value they find in the product and how they would feel if they could no longer use it. Then be honest with yourself when measuring those responses.

“If you’re 15%, 14%, 13%, or below, consider a complete pivot. Take the codebase, take the team, build something entirely new. “But if you’re 20%, you can totally optimize your way from 20% to 40%,” Vohra said.

Actually, Dham said, it’s important for a founder not to confuse having a vision with having a good business.

At the seed level especially, Barudvaj said that it’s fine to pivot. She doesn’t even look for product-market fit at that stage, but “does the founder have a thesis that seems plausible and do they have the agility to duck and wave as the situation changes?” she said.

Dham added that he values founders even more these days who have made numerous pivots because it shows they’ve had to make very hard decisions in this ever-shifting moment.

Product-market fit, therefore, is something founders will always have to redefine and re-earn. “Even at a billion in revenue, these companies are re-earning their product-market fit,” he said. “You constantly have to be innovating on products.”

articles.title: Startups don’t need to go viral to win customers
articles.summary: At TechCrunch Disrupt last week, two founders and a VC discussed how to not just gain an early following but keep one.
articles.body:
Getting initial customers as a startup can be one of the most grueling challenges in business. Even when companies manage to snag some early interest, there’s no guarantee those customers will stick around.

At TechCrunch Disrupt last week, Elia Wallen, founder and CEO of travel startup Engine, Gamma founder and CEO Grant Lee, and Crystal Huang, general partner at Google Ventures, shared tips on how to attract and retain customers.

In the current era — when young AI companies like Cluely and Instinct are building big audiences not just through their products but also through their founders’ colorful online presences — social media can seem like a magic bullet for reaching early customers. But founders who want heighten their business strategy with modern marketing, have to be strategic, according to Lee.

Gamma, which sells AI-powered presentation software, managed to scale its business exponentially with a social media strategy that deployed influencers through its Ambassadors (or “Gambassador”) program. The company adopted the plan before influencer-based marketing was a tried-and-true strategy for smaller companies, eventually reaching a multi-billion dollar valuation .

But simply giving influencers a platform and telling them to promote your brand online doesn’t automatically translate to sales, said Lee. There’s more to it than that.

“If you have a product that can serve many different segments or use cases, then you want to basically have creators that can target each one of those,” Lee said. “If you have folks that are in consulting versus people that do all their marketing and create all the decks for their CMO, there’s all these different segments you might want to go after.”

Lee said sometimes founders seem to treat creator marketing or influencer marketing as a sort of set it and forget it thing.

“I think you’re better served by really spending a lot of time with these creators, because if they’re not able to understand how to articulate the value of your product, it doesn’t matter how much money you spend, it’s just going to fall flat,” Lee added.

The effectiveness of social media depends largely on the type of business. Other ways of reaching customers can be just (if not more) effective.

Wallen would know. His company Engine, which manages lodging and travel bookings for midsize businesses, bootstrapped its way to $150 million in bookings before taking on any outside funding. They also had no visible social media strategy at all. For Wallen, traditional sales tactics can be far more useful than a positive TikTok video.

“We did events and we smiled and dialed,” said Wallen. “We still have a lot of people picking up the phone. A lot of people who didn’t grow up with that or don’t understand it think that it’s outdated or it doesn’t work but it does. It’s a hard thing. There are a lot of companies that just refuse to do it or don’t know how to do it well. But they’re missing out on a very big offline client base.” He added: “The phone still works.”

Wallen also shared an in-person tactic that his company deployed during its scrappy early days: hiring a magician named David to perform tricks for prospective clients at events and encourage them to visit the Engine’s booth. In short, old-fashioned personal engagement can work just as well, if not better, than the latest social media tricks.

Huang, who has managed droves of startups and shepherded them to success, said that once you have a customer, a lot of value can be derived from looking at how they use the product.

“Can you look into usage data and figure out if it’s recurring, if it’s increasing, if they are referring their friends?” Huang said. “It can come across in early usage and retention information as well. And then also, do you see some super fans, right, who even want to work at the company, promote the company, be attached to the brand?” She added: “You need to have ways to create evangelists who are really passionate about the product.”

articles.title: Engineer sues datacenter developer Nscale as it gets ready for listing on New York stock exchange; claims fired over letter to HR complaining over …
articles.summary: United Kingdom-based artificial intelligence infrastructure provider Nscale is facing a wrongful dismissal lawsuit in Norway.
articles.body: United Kingdom-based artificial intelligence infrastructure provider Nscale is facing a wrongful dismissal lawsuit in Norway. According to a report in Bloomberg, a former data center engineer has alleged in a lawsuit that the UK-based datacenter developer has utilized an illegal subcontracting setup. The lawsuit, filed on October 16 in the Sr-Rogaland District Court and backed by local trade unions, names both Nscale and staffing subcontractor CloudBrothers as defendants.According to the complaint reviewed by Bloomberg, the engineer claims that while he was placed at Nscale’s Stavanger facility through CloudBrothers, Nscale acted as his de facto employer by directly dictating his day-to-day duties and shift schedules. Under Norwegian labor law, subcontracting arrangements require staffing companies to manage personnel independently; end clients that treat subcontracted personnel as direct extensions of their own workforce are legally required to grant them full employee rights and compensation.The engineer alleges his June dismissal came as retaliation after he objected to employment practices at the facility. Tensions surfaced when CloudBrothers human resources reportedly told employees that two weeks of holiday pay would be withheld if vacation requests were submitted late. "You cannot deduct our worked salary," the engineer replied in an email copying the entire team, the complaint states.After subsequently raising concerns regarding pay and labor conditions with the Norwegian Labor Inspection Authority, the engineer was terminated. While CloudBrothers stated the dismissal was prompted by repeated confidentiality breaches, the suit claims the firing was retaliatory. The engineer is seeking financial compensation, damages, and a formal judicial declaration recognizing him as an official Nscale employee.Nscale and CloudBrothers did not immediately respond to requests for comment from Bloomberg. Nscale previously confirmed it had cut ties in Stavanger with another contractor, Technimove, which had placed staff through CloudBrothers.Lawsuit comes at Nscale gets ready for NYSE listingThe legal action underscores the mounting operational strains confronting Nscale as it scrambles to construct facilities to fulfill more than $100 billion in contractual obligations ahead of a planned initial public offering (IPO) in New York Stock Exchange.Nscale, which rents out computing power for training and running AI models, filed for its IPO in September. According to its IPO filing, it had $103.4 billion in signed and active contracts at the end of August this year. The company reportedly plans to list on the New York Stock Exchange under the ticker NSCL and raise up to $3bn.Norway serves as a key pillar in Nscale's European roadmap, driven by access to competitive hydropower. Backed by major shareholder Aker AS, the company operates across sites in Stavanger, Glomfjord, Oslo, and Narvik. However, rapid scaling has brought complications; There have been reports of equipment malfunctions, cooling leaks, and safety issues at Nscale's Glomfjord location.Adding to the Nscale's woes, Microsoft has reportedly pulled out of a deal to be the main tenant at the company's planned data centre in Loughton, Essex. The software giant Microsoft reportedly made the decision to exit after grid operators said that they do not expect to supply power to the site until the 2030s.You use AI every day. articles.title: US military has a 'dog problem' that goes to Europe, Palmer Luckey has a plan to solve it: Genetically engineered clone dogs of …
articles.summary: The US military relies heavily on working dogs for missions ranging from explosives detection to security operations, but according to a new Fortune
articles.body: The US military relies heavily on working dogs for missions ranging from explosives detection to security operations, but according to a new Fortune report, America is facing a growing shortage of suitable military canines. Now, a new defence technology startup backed by prominent Silicon Valley investors believes it has a solution: genetically engineered, cloned military dogs equipped with advanced protective gear and integrated with battlefield technologies. As per the Fortune report, Warhound, a new Texas-based defence startup conceived by Anduril founder Palmer Luckey and Colossal Biosciences CEO Ben Lamm, has emerged from stealth mode with a $200 million seed funding round. The company aims to use cloning and gene-editing technologies to create healthier, more capable working dogs while reducing the U.S. military's dependence on European breeders.America's dependence on European military dogsAccording to the report, more than 80% of U.S. military working dogs are currently sourced from Europe. The Pentagon's Military Working Dog Program operates more than 2,200 dog teams, but finding suitable animals has become increasingly difficult. Lamm told Fortune that the United States is competing with foreign governments, including China and Russia, to acquire top-quality dogs from a limited pool of overseas breeders. The challenge is compounded by the fact that less than half of the dogs purchased ultimately qualify for military service after completing a lengthy training and evaluation process.As a result, the military reportedly needs to purchase and train around 200 dogs to eventually field 100 operational working animals, significantly increasing costs and logistical challenges.How the plan worksLamm's confidence in the project stems from technology developed at Colossal Biosciences, the company known for its high-profile de-extinction efforts. Earlier this year, Colossal announced the creation of animals carrying genetic traits inspired by the extinct dire wolf through gene-editing and cloning techniques.Lamm described the approach in stages. Warhound will find top dogs that have finished training and bank their genetic material. It will then clone those proven animals, though Lamm acknowledged that training and environment will always influence performance. In parallel, the company will pursue targeted gene edits. The first group of dogs has already been banked and is being edited, and Lamm expects to deliver the first dogs in about two years.Edits will first aim to screen out known harmful variants linked to muscle degeneration and other inherited diseases, so that no dog enters service carrying markers for common career-ending conditions. Lamm said the company is still deciding which other traits are scientifically and responsibly actionable, but is planning future genetic enhancements to improve performance."The first group of dogs has already been biobanked and is being edited now," Lamm told Fortune, adding that the company expects its first dogs to be delivered within approximately two years.Gene editing aimed at healthier service animalsWarhound says its initial focus will be eliminating known genetic conditions linked to issues such as muscle degeneration and other inherited diseases that can prematurely end a dog's military career. Lamm said the company is still determining which additional characteristics can be responsibly enhanced through biotechnology, but acknowledged that Warhound is considering future genetic modifications to improve performance beyond current standards.The company argues that reducing genetic health risks could increase the number of dogs capable of successfully completing demanding military training programmes.Anduril brings the hardwareWhile Colossal's technology forms the biological foundation of the project, Luckey's defence company Anduril will contribute the equipment layer. Warhound plans to equip dogs with protective technologies including body armour, eye and hearing protection, and integration with Anduril's Eagle Eye situational awareness platform. The company describes these systems as "cybernetic augments" designed to allow dogs, handlers and autonomous systems to operate as a coordinated team.Despite the futuristic vision, Lamm rejected suggestions that the programme is a stepping stone toward robotic replacements. "No machine today matches a dog's nose or its judgment in complex environments," he said.A subscription model for military dogsWarhound has not yet secured official customers and has not disclosed pricing. However, the company is reportedly exploring a "Canine-as-a-Service" model in which government agencies would pay for a continuous supply of trained and supported working dogs rather than purchasing individual animals.The approach mirrors subscription-based procurement models increasingly used across the defence technology sector. The startup's investors include In-Q-Tel, Sequoia Capital, ARK Invest, Franklin Templeton, 8VC, Breyer Capital, Lux Capital and several other venture firms.The 'Captain America dog program'Lamm described the concept as something akin to a "Captain America dog program," referencing the comic-book super-soldier project that transformed Steve Rogers into Captain America. According to Lamm, the idea emerged during a conversation with Luckey at entrepreneur Peter Diamandis' Moonshots Summit, where the two discussed military dog shortages, high training failure rates and growing procurement costs.Although Luckey helped develop the concept, Lamm stressed that Warhound operates independently. Former Pentagon Chief Data Officer David Spirk, a Marine veteran with extensive experience in defence and intelligence organisations, has been appointed CEO and will lead the company as it seeks to turn biotechnology research into field-ready military capabilities. articles.title: These clever apps show off the iPhone Duo's potential | TechCrunch
articles.summary: From retro cassette players and virtual notebooks to flight trackers and even a digital toaster, developers are finding creative ways to take advantage of Apple's first foldable iPhone.
articles.body:
It’s been a long time since I’ve been genuinely excited about a new iPhone.

For years, a new iPhone meant a device that was thinner, faster, and had a camera that came with incredible upgrades. At some point (and Apple devotees can debate which year’s model this was!), a new iPhone became an incremental upgrade. Slightly better, slightly faster. Maybe there was a new button to learn, a new charging cable , or a new notch on the screen , but the iPhone itself remained the same rectangular glass and metal handheld it always was.

The iPhone Duo changes this, allowing Apple to enter the market for foldable phones with a phone that, while imperfect , is whimsical, fun, and, yes, actually exciting.

It’s hard to say when the urge to acquire the iPhone Duo first kicked in. I’ll admit that it wasn’t during the official announcement , which left me feeling puzzled about the device’s potential. Do I actually want a phone that folds, I wondered? Was propping up the phone as a little tent to watch Netflix worth all that extra money? (The Duo starts at $2,000).

As it turned out, the desire for the Duo grew on me as I saw developers embracing the new foldable design to create Duo-optimized apps. Apple’s software development community, after all, is what keeps me locked into the iPhone. Apple developers are active, creative, engaged, and still often build for iOS first – a must if you like trying things early.

Of course, the initial Duo reviews have pointed out how many mainstream iOS apps have not yet been made ready for the Duo, which is true. Many of the apps you use every day were not optimized by launch day, meaning they’re surrounded by black bars, have their controls in odd places, or have to be enlarged with a tap, similar to the early days of running iPhone apps on iPad.

But the developers who have specifically built for the Duo sparked my interest. Soon, my inbox was filled with pitches for clever apps I couldn’t yet try unless I got my hands on a Duo. Hello, FOMO.

The best of these don’t just adapt their apps to display correctly on the foldable form factor, but make use of the fact that there are different displays of different sizes – and they incorporate that into the design of the apps themselves.

Below are some of my early favorites, tested on a review unit provided by Apple.

Let’s start with the basics. Netflix is one of Apple’s hand-picked partners for the Duo launch, and had its streaming app Duo-optimized by the time the device shipped, alongside others like the MLB app, NYT Cooking, Slack, my preferred calendar app Fantastical , and others. But Netflix is the perfect showcase for what I expect will be a regular Duo use case: watching movies and TV.

The streaming app hasn’t just been expanded to fill the screen; it takes advantage of the fact that there are two different screen sizes to build for. On the outer screen (the display you see when the device is folded), you can scroll through Netflix’s short-form, TikTok-like “Clips,” then open up the device to continue watching videos on the larger matte-screen inner display. The transition between the two experiences feels as seamless as unfolding the Duo itself, as the content automatically adapts to the new screen size.

As I personally find myself watching most TV on my phone these days, as opposed to big screen in the living room, I appreciate having the option to shift from a phone to a larger screen with one device. This is going to be one of my most-used apps, I think.

Look, I called it back in September. I have to credit Deck-Man , which was previously known as Duo-Man, as being the first app that made me want to get a Duo. Designed by indie developer Vidit Bhargava at a hackathon, the music player takes clever advantage of the Duo’s two screens to imitate how Walkman cassette players used to function.

The playful app reimagines the cassette player as a digital experience with retro vibes, allowing you to browse through your favorite albums as cassettes, then load them into the player. You can then control the playback with play, pause, fast-forward, and rewind controls, as you would on a hardware device, complete with authentic-sounding clicks and cassette sounds that were recorded from a real portable cassette player.

With the Duo open, the cassette appears to play on the right side of the screen, next to album imagery on the right. When closed, Deck-Man’s interface looks like the front of a Walkman.

The app has appeal not only because it built something that could only exist on a hinged, foldable device like the Duo, but also because it taps into the growing demand for retro tech , which is partly a cultural response to the speed at which the AI industry is shipping out products. Retro tech , like dumbphones , digital cameras, vinyl, CDs , and landlines, recalls an older time when tech use was intentional, not just baked into every aspect of our lives.

Honestly, if you buy a Duo and don’t install Deck-Man, I’m convinced you just don’t know how to have fun.

The TypeDraw app is designed to be a personal notebook, something that looks like a virtual Moleskine of sorts — it even has an elastic closure band. But there’s a certain charm to using this app specifically on the Duo, whose form factor makes it look a lot like a little notebook when closed.

Inside TypeDraw, you can type using a font that’s your own handwriting or pick from one of a dozen fonts designed by its creator, Phil Traut.

You can also choose which kind of paper you want to write on, like lined, grid, or dotted pages, and pick your ink color. You can also draw and sketch to create colorful images that accompany your handwritten text, which makes it feel a lot more like using a real-life notebook as your journal or diary, and not some boring to-do app.

The pages curl as you flip through them, and you can even pull on the elastic band to produce a twang animation that’s just silly and fun.

Wakeout , the workout app that’s a former Apple App of the Year winner, has also approached its Duo optimization thoughtfully by designing different user interfaces for each postion the phone can be in. The app, which offers a series of mini movement breaks that feel more like games than exercise, works when the Duo is closed, open, in tent mode, or sitting open like a laptop computer.

For instance, when the Duo is open like a book, the view is split across the hinge with the movement game videos on the left, but when it’s open like a laptop, the videos shift to the vertical screen. You can also put it into tent mode, which is great for watching the videos with the Duo propped up on your desk. (Most people use Wakeout at work, when they take quick stretch breaks after sitting at a desk for too long.)

If the app is running on a closed Duo, its row of navigation tabs becomes a slim side menu in the column beside the camera, allowing the phone’s small screen to use the full display.

Already my favorite travel app, Apple Design Award-winning Flighty tells you everything you need to know about your upcoming flight, from gate updates to delays to airport conditions and even the type of aircraft you’re flying.

But on the iPhone Duo, when open, the app takes advantage of the expanded screen space to spread its map to the edges, letting you see more of your flight’s path on a globe that spins under your fingertips.

When the Duo is open, your flight details move over to the left side of the screen, but it doesn’t fill that side of the screen. Instead, most of the display is taken up by the image of the globe, allowing you room to zoom in on different flight paths more closely as you plan your travels.

The app also works in split screen, which means you can keep track of your flight while also doing something else — like watching your favorite TV show.

Plus, Flighty added a new feature called En Route Mode just for the Duo. In this mode, the Duo is folded into the tent shape and then placed on a flat surface — like your airplane’s tray table. That way you can watch your flight’s progress via Wi-Fi while you do something else, like listen to music, read a book, or watch a movie from the in-flight entertainment’s seat-back screen.

Designed specifically for the Duo (and for tech enthusiasts, who are also the Duo’s first customers), Tiny Computers is a playful way to reconnect with older technology. The app ships with 10 retro computers that you can play with, including the Macintosh, Commodore 64, IBM PC, Amiga 500, Windows 95, ThinkPad, iMac G3, iBook G3, PowerBook G4, and Windows XP.

You’re meant to set up the Duo in its open “laptop” mode to toy around with these old-fashioned devices, which feature clicking keyboards, working command lines, paint programs, floppy disks, and even some desktop games. But it’s not just an old computer exhibit – there’s a game element too, as you can look for hidden files and secret commands to earn a medal.

There are no ads, subscriptions, or in-app purchases, either – just a $3.99 one-time fee.

Sky Guide is that classic stargazing app that I still open from time to time when I’m outdoors enjoying nature, wondering whether that bright light up there is a star or a planet or what the constellation right next to Orion is called.

The company is another of those that Apple gave a shoutout to in its press release about all the new Duo-optimized apps, and it’s easy to see why. It’s just so much easier to track the night sky when you have the larger display on the Duo unfolded, offering a more immersive, edge-to-edge map that moves as your position and orientation change. This one will be broken out on the next camping trip or nighttime walk, for sure.

Maybe I’m just a sucker for retro music apps, but MD Vinyl did not disappoint with its Duo-optimized music player.

This app’s widget already has a permanent place on my regular iPhone’s Home Screen purely for the aesthetics, which includes a tiny, spinning record and a display that shows you the song title and artist you’re streaming, alongside the player controls.

Now for the iPhone Duo, the virtual vinyl record gets to use more of the screen. Plus, you can even pick up the record player’s arm and place it on the spinning disk to start the music or remove it to stop it.

Before the Duo, Pico Cam offered a tiny, playful camera app for taking virtual Polaroid-style pictures, which eject from the phone’s Dynamic Island (the pill-shaped cutout at the top of the screen). You can also shake the picture to get it to develop faster, then decorate with little stickers and share with friends.

Now optimized for the iPhone Duo, Pico Cam can be used when the phone is both open and closed, with the latter giving you more screen space to see your photo gallery after pictures are taken.

Remember when the iPhone first came out, and there was that app that would make it look like you were drinking a beer when you tilted the phone to your mouth? Toastie is the iPhone Duo version of that same type of ridiculous experience.

I wouldn’t call Toastie a “killer” app, of course; it’s far too silly for that. But it’s a pretty fun toy to play with — if you ever dare to hand over this expensive device to a kid.

The app, cheekily described as the “world’s most expensive toaster” (a reference to the Duo’s exorbitant price), lets you follow a recipe to create a piece of toast with butter, cheese, or any of the other numerous toppings, then close the Duo to let the toast cook.

Open the phone too soon, and your toast will be undercooked, losing you the 5-star review you’re after.

You definitely don’t need this app, but what’s another $2.99 when you’ve already dropped a bundle on the phone itself?

We expect more interesting apps to come as developers get their hands on the iPhone Duo in the weeks ahead.

articles.title: Instacart reportedly discussed selling itself with DoorDash and Uber
articles.summary: Instacart might sell itself to a larger competitor.
articles.body:
Instacart might sell itself to a larger competitor, according to multiple news reports

The Information reported Friday that the grocery delivery company has hired an investment bank to help it evaluate its options, and that it’s held acquisition talks with DoorDash. And Bloomberg reported that the company has also talked to Uber — although Uber reportedly walked away from those discussions.

Instacart currently has a market cap of more than $13 billion, and its stock price is up 25% for the year to date. The company could see this as a good time to sell at a desirable price, before the grocery delivery market gets more competitive — but Bloomberg noted that these are early discussions that might not result in a sale.

An Instacart spokesperson declined to comment. The reports of a potential sale caused the company’s share price to spike more than 9.2% on Friday, while Uber and DoorDash stock declined.

articles.title: TechCrunch Mobility: Blue-green is the color of autonomy | TechCrunch
articles.summary: Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility, your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it.
articles.body:
Welcome back to TechCrunch Mobility , your hub for the future of transportation and now, more than ever, the role AI is playing in it. To get this in your inbox, sign up here for free — just click TechCrunch Mobility !

U.S. federal safety regulators continue to tackle the sticky problem of autonomous vehicles, this time with a proposal that could signal to the public, quite literally, when a vehicle is operating autonomously.

The National Highway Traffic Safety Administration has proposed new lighting requirements for autonomous vehicles that include an option (dare I say a strong suggestion?) to use cyan-colored lights to signal when a vehicle is operating autonomously without a human occupant monitoring the road.

The agency is not proposing a mandate for blue-green lights. Importantly, under the proposal, the lights would be used when an AV is operating in autonomous mode.

Still, federal regulators are clearly seeking some uniform way of identifying autonomous vehicles.

The proposal establishes equipment specifications, including where the lights are mounted, the color they emit, and how they’re activated. It would also remove requirements for manually operated controls for turn signals, high beams, and hazard lights.

Under the proposal, the NHTSA suggests the lights be cyan (blue-green), remain steadily illuminated rather than flash, and be visible from the front, rear, and both sides.

This latest proposal is one piece of a bigger effort to update regulations that help speed up the adoption of AVs while maintaining safety, according to NHTSA administrator Jonathan Morrison.

The agency is already working on a federal automated vehicle framework and is trying to update federal motor vehicle safety standards, which already govern automakers today. For instance, FMVSS rules were not designed for vehicles like the Tesla Cybercab and Zoox robotaxi, which lack traditional, federally required equipment like pedals, steering wheels, and design features like side mirrors and rearview mirrors.

While the feds wrestle over regulating the future of transportation, GM laid out how it plans to be part of it. The automaker held its annual GM Forward event, and a lot of what was announced builds on last year’s push into AI. But now we have more details and dates.

The U.S. automaker is overhauling the electrical and computational guts of its future vehicles in a bid to deliver faster software, more capable automated driving features, and a custom, conversational AI assistant that will change its 30-year-old OnStar service.

This technological overhaul is set to debut in 2028 with the Cadillac Escalade IQ. The company will also roll out an autonomous highway driving feature in 2028 that will allow drivers to have their hands and eyes off the road and without the need to be ready to take over.

GM has also adopted enterprise AI across the company to slash its traditional four- to five-year development timeline in half.

I have been around long enough to remember previous efforts at GM and other legacy automakers, all of which were interpreted as a bid to compete with Tesla. This time, GM seems to be preparing for a bigger fight.

AI startups are getting snapped up across industries, including transportation. The latest example is Rivian’s acquisition of Third Dimension , a U.K. startup founded by veterans of the gaming and autonomous vehicle industries that uses AI to turn images and videos into lifelike 3D worlds.

This is all about simulation, and specifically the idea of taking driving data and bringing it into a virtual world that matches the physical world. Rivian’s head of autonomy, James Philbin, told me the company knew it needed a technology that could close the “sim-to-real gap,” meaning the data gap between real and simulated environments.

Students of the AV industry will likely shout “Simulation is so 2017!” And yes, that’s true, simulation is a tool AV developers have relied on and continue to do so. The technology behind simulation continues to evolve, and startups like Third Dimension are ripe for the picking.

The terms of the deal weren’t released. There are a few clues for what size of deal this may have been. Third Dimension previously raised a $7 million seed round, and it has about 15 engineers, and Rivian didn’t disclose this in an SEC filing (meaning it didn’t hit the bar for material information).

Ride-hailing company inDrive , known for letting passengers and drivers negotiate fares, is working with Chinese autonomous driving firm Pony.ai and Nvidia to begin testing robotaxis in Kazakhstan in 2027. The companies have signed a memorandum of understanding to explore bringing Pony.ai’s robotaxis to inDrive’s platform.

Reliable Robotics , a startup trying to commercialize autonomous flying technology that can be installed on existing aircraft, raised $115 million . The Series D extension round included $90 million in equity funding led by Nimble Partners and $25 million in debt from Silicon Valley Bank. The Series D round now totals $275 million and has pushed the startup’s valuation beyond the $1 billion mark.

A group fighting robotaxis has some mysterious origins, the Washington Post reported . This reminds me of another anti-robotaxi group that I dug into earlier this summer called Coalition for Accountability and Road Safety, which was canvassing voters and posting on social media. My reporting discovered that the organization was registered to an employee of a New York lobbying firm that has previously been retained by several labor unions and the New York Black Car Operators’ Injury Compensation Fund.

GM is closing a plant south of Detroit that assembled battery packs for Cadillac’s flagship EV, the Celestiq, and both electric drive units and battery packs for the plug-in hybrid Chevrolet Corvette E-Ray. The closure is not related to GM’s electric vehicle strategy but because the lease on the site was nearing its end, according to a GM spokesperson.

Google is upgrading Gemini in vehicles with a personal intelligence feature that can draw on information from Gmail, Google Calendar, YouTube, Maps, Google Search history, and other connected Google services to understand your preferences, activities, and past experiences.

Rivian CEO RJ Scaringe shared his vision for how autonomy will allow his company to build radically different kinds of vehicles than the R1S electric pickup truck and R1S and R2 SUVs it makes today. All eyes are on R4.

Tesla and SpaceX reported third-quarter earnings this week, and comments by Elon Musk, who is CEO of both companies, has kicked merger talk into fifth gear. Musk said the boards of each company have formed special committees to review a merger.

Meanwhile, SpaceX’s AI business is booming , generating $7.5 billion in revenue, and now makes up 52% of the company’s income. And Tesla’s revenue, across its segments, was flat, while the company’s expenses grew. The upshot: Profits fell 43% year-over-year. Musk is very much focused on the company’s AI and robotics future, though. Tesla started production of its Optimus humanoid robot, reported rosy FSD subscription growth even as the “unsupervised version” was delayed to Q2 next year, and said it plans to start selling its Cybercab to customers by the end of the year. As senior reporter Sean O’Kane wrote: Tesla is prepping for a Cybercab onslaught .

Waymo keeps expanding within cities it already operates and into new ones. The company said it plans to launch a robotaxi service in Spain, starting with Madrid. It expects to open it up to riders in 2027. Closer to home, Waymo is now shuttling customers to and from the Harry Reid International Airport in Las Vegas.

TechCrunch Disrupt just wrapped and I am already preparing for another event. This time, it is the Founder Summit — a one-day event in Boston focused on, you guessed it, founders. This event, taking place November 4, is valuable for startup founders, aspiring founders, and investors. Attendees can expect advice-driven talks from VCs and serial founders, plus lots of chances to network.

And I will be there! Come say hi. To help make that happen, I will give TechCrunch Mobility readers a 30% discount on tickets. Click this link and use the code mobility30.
